strengths: Addresses a practically important EDA problem (fast RTL quality estimation without invoking synthesis) with a well-motivated argument that CDFGs expose structural semantics more explicitly than token sequences used by prior LLM-based methods.

The two pretraining objectives (structure-aware masked node modeling on post-GNN embeddings, and edge prediction) are a thoughtful adaptation of graph SSL to CDFGs, explicitly designed to avoid the semantic ambiguity that arises from masking raw operator nodes/edges in computational graphs -- a reasonable and somewhat novel technical insight.

Combines structural pretraining with a cross-stage knowledge distillation strategy from post-mapping netlists, and shows this benefits both the proposed method and all baselines, supporting the claim that cross-stage supervision is broadly useful.

Dataset scale (13,200 designs) is substantially larger than earlier hand-crafted-feature works (<100 designs), improving the credibility of generalization claims relative to prior graph-based baselines.

Reasonably thorough experimental comparison against both graph-based (XGBoost, GNN) and LLM-based (CodeV variants) baselines, with an ablation isolating the contribution of each pretraining task and consistent gains reported across MAE/MAPE/R2/RRSE for both area and delay, with and without KD.
weaknesses: No reported variance across seeds/splits, no significance testing, and only a single 80/20 train/val split is used -- given regression metrics with claimed ~0.1 R2 improvements, it is unclear whether these gains are robust or within noise, especially since neural training on this scale can be sensitive to initialization.

The comparison to VeriDistill is indirect: the paper reimplements CodeV embeddings with its own MLP head rather than reproducing VeriDistill's exact pipeline/dataset/splits, and it is unclear whether the same train/val partition, hyperparameter tuning effort, and preprocessing were applied equally to baselines and StructRTL, raising concerns about a fair and reproducible comparison.

Key hyperparameters (mask ratio 20%, k=16 eigenvectors, α=0.5, τ=0.7, μ=0.5, minimum-per-class m in stratified masking) are fixed without ablation or sensitivity analysis, making it hard to assess robustness of the design choices and reproducibility of the reported gains.
The anonymized code/data repository link in the Appendix is left blank/placeholder, undermining reproducibility claims despite the paper's assertion that code is available.

MasterRTL, a directly relevant prior graph-based PPA estimation baseline discussed at length in Related Work, is excluded from the empirical comparison (justified only by its use of a bit-level, post-some-synthesis representation), leaving a gap versus the closest prior structural-feature approach.

No analysis of inference-time/computational efficiency versus LLM-based baselines, which would strengthen the paper's core motivating claim of enabling 'instant feedback' compared to LLM embedding extraction or full synthesis.

Technology-library generalization is untested: all synthesis/KD experiments use a single PDK (SkyWater 130nm), so it's unclear whether the learned structural representations and distillation benefits transfer to other libraries or technology nodes.

Limited discussion of failure modes, scalability to very large designs (up to 19k nodes CDFGs), or cases where structural pretraining might not help (e.g., very small or highly regular designs), despite dataset statistics suggesting a long tail in design size.

strengths: The paper is well motivated: it makes a reasonable case that CDFGs expose structural semantics that a token-based LLM view does not, and that generation-focused LLM pretraining may be poorly matched to quality-estimation objectives.

The proposed adaptation of masked modeling and edge prediction to operate on post-GNN context-aware embeddings (rather than raw node/edge masking as in GraphMAE/MaskGAE) is a sensible engineering response to the semantic ambiguity of masking operator nodes in a CDFG.

The class imbalance in CDFG node types is explicitly addressed via stratified masking and class-balanced focal loss, which is a reasonable practical fix given the node-type distribution reported in the appendix.
The knowledge distillation from a post-mapping netlist teacher to the CDFG student is a reasonable cross-stage supervision idea and is evaluated with and without this component.
The dataset (13,200 designs) is larger than those used in some prior graph-based baselines and the paper reports dataset/label statistics in the appendix.
Ablations for the two pretraining losses (w/o Lmnm, w/o Lep) are included in both KD and no-KD settings.
weaknesses: Only a single train/validation split (0.8:0.2) is used throughout; no cross-validation, multiple seeds, or reported variance/confidence intervals are given, making it hard to assess whether the reported R2 gains (e.g., ~0.1 improvement) are statistically robust rather than a product of a particular split.

Several architectural claims are asserted without ablation support: e.g., the paper states that omitting global positional embeddings 'would' cause training collapse, but no experiment demonstrating this is shown; similarly, the choice of k=16 eigenvectors, alpha=0.5, tau=0.7, mu=0.5 are all fixed without any sensitivity analysis or justification.

MasterRTL, a directly relevant prior graph-based PPA estimation method discussed at length in Related Work, is excluded from the empirical comparison with a somewhat convenient rationale (that its SOG representation requires synthesis steps); given the paper's stated goal of establishing new SOTA, this omission is not fully justified since a comparison (even if the setting differs) would strengthen the significance argument.

The core technical contribution is largely a recombination and domain adaptation of existing ingredients (GIN + Transformer with Laplacian PE from GraphGPS, GraphMAE-style masked modeling, MaskGAE-style edge prediction, VeriDistill-style KD, class-balanced focal loss from prior CV work), so originality is more incremental engineering integration than a fundamentally new method or insight.

The LLM-based baselines are limited to three CodeV variants (<=7B); no comparison to more recent/larger Verilog-specialized LLM embedding methods (e.g., DeepRTL/DeepRTL2, which are cited but not benchmarked) is provided, which weakens the claim of a comprehensive comparison against 'prior art'.

No runtime/latency comparison is reported despite the central motivating claim of the paper being fast feedback compared to full logic synthesis and compared to LLM-based embedding extraction; this leaves the practical speed-accuracy trade-off unsubstantiated.

Dataset construction from GitHub/textbook sources raises potential concerns about near-duplicate or highly similar designs across the train/validation split (module-level or repository-level leakage), which is not discussed or controlled for, and could inflate reported performance.

The paper reports validation accuracies for the pretraining tasks (82.27%, 95.77%) but does not analyze failure modes, per-class performance for underrepresented node types, or whether stratified masking/focal loss actually closes the imbalance gap in results.

Presentation of results emphasizes R2 as the primary metric with a somewhat informal justification ('provides insight into relative quality'), while other metrics (MAPE, RRSE) sometimes show less consistent improvement patterns that are not discussed.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap: prior LLM-based RTL quality estimators operate on token sequences and largely discard explicit structural information, whereas CDFGs expose control/data dependencies directly; the paper provides a clear, intuitive rationale for why this should help, particularly for delay prediction which depends heavily on structural path length.

The two pretraining tasks are thoughtfully adapted to the peculiarities of computational graphs: masking is applied at the level of post-GNN context-aware embeddings rather than raw node/edge features, explicitly avoiding the ambiguity problem that would arise from masking, e.g., an arithmetic operator in a CDFG. This is a sensible and non-trivial adaptation of GraphMAE/MaskGAE ideas to a domain with strict functional semantics.

The paper identifies and handles a genuine practical challenge (severe class imbalance across 32 CDFG node types) with two concrete mechanisms (stratified masking, class-balanced focal loss), and validates their necessity via ablation (removing either pretraining loss degrades performance in both the w/o KD and w/ KD settings).

Dataset scale (13,200 designs) is substantially larger than earlier hand-crafted-feature works (<100 designs) and comparable to the VeriDistill-scale evaluation, improving credibility of the reported trends.

Reasonably comprehensive baseline suite: hand-crafted-feature (Graph-XGBoost), end-to-end GNN without pretraining (Graph-GNN), and three LLM-embedding variants (CodeV-DS/CL/QW), plus a knowledge-distillation study showing consistent gains from cross-stage (PM netlist) supervision across all methods, not just StructRTL, which strengthens the case that KD contributes a real, generalizable signal.

Clear architectural motivation for structural (Laplacian-based) positional embeddings when flattening a graph into a Transformer sequence, together with a sign-flip augmentation to address eigenvector sign ambiguity.
weaknesses: No variance/uncertainty reporting: all results appear to be single-run point estimates (Tables 1 and 2) with no standard deviations, multiple seeds, or significance tests, making it hard to assess whether the reported margins (e.g., 0.02–0.05 R^2 differences between StructRTL and best baselines with KD) are robust or within noise.

The core motivation of the paper is faster feedback than full logic synthesis, yet no wall-clock/runtime comparison is provided between StructRTL inference (including CDFG construction via Yosys + Stagira parsing) versus token-based LLM embedding extraction versus full synthesis. Without this, the practical 'speed' claim central to the introduction is not empirically substantiated.

Key design choices and hyperparameters (k=16 eigenvectors, mask ratio 20%, alpha=0.5, tau=0.7, mu=0.5, focal-loss beta/gamma) are fixed without sensitivity analysis or ablation, so it is unclear how much of the performance depends on careful tuning versus the proposed mechanisms themselves.

The claim that global positional embeddings are 'vital' and their absence causes 'training collapse' is asserted but not empirically demonstrated with an ablation removing them, unlike the two pretraining losses which are ablated.
Reproducibility artifact is incomplete: the anonymous GitHub link in the Appendix is blank, so the implementation and dataset cannot currently be verified or accessed by reviewers/readers.

Train/validation split is a simple random 80/20 split of GitHub/textbook-sourced designs; there is no discussion of potential near-duplicate or template-similar designs leaking across the split (a known issue with GitHub-scraped HDL corpora such as VeriGen/DeepCircuitX), which could inflate reported performance.

Only one technology library (SkyWater 130nm) and one synthesis toolchain (Yosys+ABC) are used for the KD teacher and ground-truth area/delay labels; generalization of the approach to other PDKs or commercial synthesis flows is unverified.

MasterRTL and PRIMAL, discussed at length in Related Work, are excluded from quantitative comparison (justified for MasterRTL due to its synthesis-dependent SOG, but PRIMAL is not addressed at all), leaving some prior structural-feature approaches uncompared.
The paper only evaluates area and delay; other commonly-relevant PPA metrics (e.g., power, as suggested by PRIMAL) are not considered despite being mentioned as motivation in the related work.

strengths: The paper convincingly motivates CDFG over token-based/AST representations for RTL quality estimation, and the empirical results (Tables 1-2) show a clear and consistent margin over both hand-crafted-feature graph baselines and strong LLM-based baselines (VeriDistill/CodeV variants), especially in delay prediction.

The pretraining objectives are thoughtfully adapted to the computational-graph domain: rather than masking raw node/edge features (which can create semantic ambiguity, e.g., masking an Add could equally be a Sub), masking is applied at the post-GNN embedding level, which is a sensible domain-specific design choice with supporting ablations (Appendix E).

Extensive supplementary experiments substantially strengthen the empirical case: architecture ablations, sensitivity to masking/sampling ratios, per-class masked-node accuracy analysis, generalization across functional clusters and design sizes, evaluation on 51 real industrial design pairs (102 modules), inference-latency/memory scaling curves, and a comparison of LLMs operating directly on CDFGs (further isolating whether gains stem from representation or minor confounds).

Dataset construction (13,200 designs from multiple public Verilog corpora, functional simulation filtering) is considerably larger than prior graph-based RTL quality-estimation work (~100 designs), improving statistical reliability of comparisons.

The knowledge distillation from post-mapping netlists is a reasonable, well-motivated mechanism for bridging the RTL-to-gate-level gap and is shown to consistently improve all methods, not just the proposed one, supporting its general validity.

The limitations section (Appendix O) is candid about scalability to very large designs, weaker performance on sequential circuits, and the open problem of cross-technology-node generalization, and proposes a concrete (if preliminary) mitigation (register-boundary partitioning).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing techniques (GraphMAE-style masked modeling, MaskGAE-style edge prediction, GPS-style Laplacian positional encodings, VeriDistill-style cross-stage KD) applied to a new representation (CDFG) rather than a fundamentally new method; the novelty is primarily in domain adaptation/engineering rather than new algorithmic insight.

Memory and runtime scale steeply with design size (52GB peak memory and ~200ms latency at 20K nodes), and the proposed mitigation (register-boundary partitioning) is only a preliminary pilot study on a small set of 51 industrial pairs without validation on very large designs (>100K nodes), leaving scalability to true industrial-scale designs unresolved.

The method is only demonstrated on a single technology library (SkyWater 130nm); cross-technology-node transfer, which the paper itself flags as important for practical EDA adoption, is not empirically evaluated, only discussed qualitatively via limited-data experiments.

Masked node modeling accuracy remains modest for many rare but functionally important operator classes (e.g., ~55-60% for comparison/shift operators even with class-balanced strategies), suggesting the self-supervised signal may be weaker than implied by the strong downstream numbers, and the paper does not analyze how per-class pretraining quality correlates with downstream error for specific operator-heavy designs.

No variance/uncertainty is reported across multiple training seeds or dataset splits for the main results (Tables 1-2), making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported R^2/RRSE improvements, particularly given some deltas versus the strongest CodeV baseline could be modest relative to potential run-to-run variance.

Industrial validation, while a nice addition, is limited to pairwise ranking accuracy on only 51 design pairs; absolute area/delay prediction errors on industrial designs (which are more relevant for early feedback use-cases) are not reported.

Reproducibility of CDFG construction relies on a specific toolchain (Yosys, Stagira Verilog parser) and undocumented implementation choices (e.g., exact node-type taxonomy of 32 classes, handling of parameterized/generate constructs), which may complicate independent replication despite the stated code release.

strengths: Constructs a substantially larger dataset (13,200 designs) than prior RTL quality-estimation work (which typically used <100 designs), improving statistical reliability of the comparison.
The CDFG-based representation is a reasonable and well-motivated alternative to token-based LLM embeddings, since it explicitly encodes control and data dependencies relevant to timing/area.

Careful engineering choices are documented: masking at the post-GNN embedding level (rather than raw node/edge masking) to avoid semantic ambiguity in computational graphs, stratified masking plus class-balanced focal loss to address severe class imbalance among node types, and sign-flipping augmentation for Laplacian positional encodings.

Extensive appendix experiments (functional-shift splits, size-based generalization, industrial pairwise ranking, runtime/memory scaling, LLM directly consuming CDFG text, fully fine-tuned LLM baseline) show an effort toward robustness checks beyond the main table.
Reports a large latency speedup (145x) versus logic synthesis, which is practically relevant for iterative EDA workflows.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the architecture is essentially a GNN + GraphGPS-style Transformer with Laplacian positional encodings (Rampášek et al., 2022) combined with masked-node and edge-prediction objectives adapted from GraphMAE/MaskGAE, and the knowledge distillation component is explicitly borrowed from VeriDistill. The contribution is largely an application/adaptation of existing techniques to a new graph domain rather than a new learning paradigm.

The paper states 'The code is open-sourced at' but no URL or anonymized repository link is actually provided anywhere in the manuscript, which is a real reproducibility gap given the many implementation-specific choices (CDFG extraction pipeline, hyperparameters, masking schedules).

All reported results appear to be from single training runs; no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported for any table, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (e.g., the ~0.04–0.05 R² improvement over the best LLM baseline once knowledge distillation is applied, Table 2) are statistically meaningful versus training noise.

Evaluation is restricted to a single technology node (SkyWater 130nm); the paper itself acknowledges that a 'universal quality estimator that generalizes...across technology nodes remains an open problem,' meaning the practical utility of the trained models beyond this specific PDK is unverified.

Performance on sequential circuits — arguably the more common and important case in real RTL design — is consistently weaker than on combinational circuits (Appendix G), and this core limitation is not addressed by any proposed mitigation beyond a suggestion for 'future work.'

The industrial evaluation is comparatively small (51 design pairs) and only reports pairwise ranking accuracy rather than the full regression metrics used elsewhere, making it harder to directly compare against the main results and raising a possibility that this particular metric was chosen because it is more forgiving.

Memory usage scales steeply with design size (52GB for a 20K-node CDFG), and the proposed register-boundary partitioning mitigation is only validated as a preliminary pilot study on the same limited industrial set, with no validation on very large designs (>100K nodes) that would stress-test real industrial scalability.

The comparison with LLM-based baselines uses frozen LLM embeddings with simple mean pooling + MLP; it is unclear whether this fully replicates the original VeriDistill training/architecture, raising a possible risk that the baseline is somewhat weakened relative to its original published form.

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: prior LLM-based RTL quality estimators rely on token-based representations that only implicitly encode structural semantics, whereas CDFGs explicitly capture control and data dependencies relevant to area/delay prediction.

The two pretraining objectives (structure-aware masked node modeling and edge prediction) are thoughtfully adapted to the computational semantics of CDFGs by masking post-GNN context-aware embeddings rather than raw node/edge attributes, avoiding the ambiguity issue that would arise from masking, e.g., an arithmetic operator directly.

Technically sound handling of graph structure: use of directed-graph Laplacian eigenvectors for global positional embeddings, sign-flipping augmentation, stratified masking, and class-balanced focal loss to address severe node-type imbalance are well-justified engineering choices with supporting ablations (Table 13, Appendix D/E/F).

Extensive and convincing empirical validation: comparisons against both hand-crafted-feature and LLM-based baselines (three CodeV variants) on a sizable dataset (13,200 designs), consistent ~0.1 R2 gains, and a broad set of appendix studies (functional-shift generalization, size-based generalization, LLM-on-CDFG, fine-tuned-LLM overfitting analysis, combinational vs. sequential breakdown).
Knowledge distillation from PM netlists is a sensible cross-stage supervision strategy and is shown to consistently improve all methods, with StructRTL still leading after KD.

Real-world relevance is demonstrated via evaluation on 51 industrial design pairs (102 modules) with meaningful ranking accuracy (82–88%) and a 145x inference speedup over synthesis, plus a runtime/memory scaling study and a preliminary but useful register-boundary partitioning strategy for scalability.

Reasonably transparent limitations section (Appendix O) that honestly discusses degraded performance on sequential circuits, scalability constraints for very large designs, and open challenges in cross-technology-node generalization, without overstating claims.
weaknesses: Absolute node-level R2 for the core (non-distilled) area/delay prediction task remains moderate (~0.75), and no error bars/multiple-seed variance are reported for the main comparisons, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains.

The industrial evaluation, while a valuable addition, is limited to only 51 design pairs (102 modules), which is a fairly small sample on which to base strong claims of industrial applicability, especially for the ranking-accuracy numbers.

Performance is noticeably weaker on sequential circuits (Appendix G), which are a substantial and important fraction of real RTL designs; the paper does not attempt any architectural remedy (e.g., temporal-aware pretraining) within the main method, only flags it as future work.

MasterRTL, a directly relevant prior SOTA method using bit-level graph representations, is excluded from comparison on the grounds that it requires synthesis-adjacent SOG construction; while a reasonable scoping decision, this leaves an important comparison point unaddressed, and other recent RTL-representation baselines (e.g., DeepRTL/DeepRTL2, cited but not benchmarked) are also omitted.

The register-boundary partitioning strategy for scalability to very large designs (>20K nodes) is explicitly described as a preliminary pilot study without validation on the largest designs of practical interest (e.g., >100K nodes), so scalability claims beyond the tested range remain speculative.

The CDFG construction pipeline depends on several external tools (Yosys, Stagira Verilog parser) and there is limited discussion of how parsing failures or unsupported RTL constructs are handled beyond simple filtering, which could affect reproducibility/robustness in more diverse industrial codebases.
